The Committee recommends that the State Party submit its combined thirteenth to fifteenth periodic reports, as a single document, by 5 October 2029, taking into account the reporting guidelines adopted by the Committee during its seventy-first session and addressing all the points raised in the present concluding observations. records.section: International Decade for People of African Descent
records.text: 49. In its resolution 79/193, the General Assembly proclaimed 2025–2034 the Second International Decade for People of African Descent. Also in that resolution, the Assembly decided to extend the programme of activities for the implementation of the International Decade for People of African Descent adopted in resolution 69/16, with a view to ensuring continuing efforts in promoting the respect, protection and fulfilment of all human rights and fundamental freedoms of people of African descent. In the light of this development, the Committee recommends that the State Party implement the programme of activities in collaboration with people of African descent and include in its next periodic report information on the measures adopted in that framework, taking into account the Committee’s general recommendation No. 34 (2011) on racial discrimination against people of African descent.

records.text: 42. The Committee recommends that the State Party conduct effective, thorough and impartial investigations into all reports of abuses and violations of human rights perpetrated against migrants, and appropriately prosecute and punish those convicted with penalties commensurate with the offences. It also recommends that the State Party provide victims of discriminatory acts and hate crimes with adequate redress and support. The Committee recommends that the State Party take effective measures to combat and monitor hate speech, incitement to and promotion of racial hatred and discrimination against migrants, including on the Internet and social media, and ensure that such incidents are effectively, thoroughly and impartially investigated and, where appropriate, prosecuted and punished with penalties commensurate with the offences.

records.text: 41. The Committee is deeply concerned about reports of an increase in hate speech and violent attacks by civilians against migrants in May 2024, leading to abuses and violations of their right to life and physical integrity and their right to the highest attainable standard of health. The Committee notes the information provided by the delegation on measures taken to address the situation, including the adoption of amendments to the Criminal Code in December 2024 to introduce harsher penalties for criminal offences against non-citizens. Nevertheless, the Committee is concerned about the lack of information on investigations into those violations and abuses, as well as the lack of opportunities for victims to seek redress and to receive support (arts. 1, 2, 4 and 6).

40. The Committee recommends that the State Party take measures to combat abuse and exploitation of migrant workers, including by assessing and reviewing the employment framework on migrant workers to reduce their vulnerability to exploitation and abuse. It also recommends that the State Party adopt measures to ensure the access of migrant workers to justice, irrespective of their status, including free legal aid, and that it conduct awareness-raising campaigns among migrant workers on their rights and on existing remedies.

records.text: 19. The Committee is concerned about the increase in restrictions imposed on exercising and enjoying the right to freedom of opinion and expression and the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association under the legislative framework and in practice. In particular, the Committee is concerned about: (a) The adoption of amendments, on 2 April 2024, to the Law on Non‐Commercial Organizations and the adoption on 27 August 2024 of the Regulation on the Procedure for Maintaining the Registry of Non-Commercial Organizations Fulfilling Functions of Foreign Representatives – negatively impacting human rights defenders and civil society organizations, in particular those working on the rights of those exposed to racial discrimination. The Committee is concerned that the recent amendments to the legislative framework allow for the labelling of civil society organizations under broad and vague concepts such as “foreign representatives” and “political activity”, the imposition of undue registration and reporting requirements and the establishment of broad governmental oversight powers over the activities of such organizations, and restrict access to funding; (b) The overly broad and vague concepts and provisions in the legislative framework that allow for arbitrary interpretations of and disproportionate restrictions on the right to freedom of expression and the right to freedom of association of members of ethnic minority groups, human rights defenders, members of civil society organizations, activists, lawyers and journalists, such as “humiliation of national dignity” in article 330 (incitement to racial, ethnic, national, religious or interregional hostility) and articles 278 (3) (calls for mass disorder), 326 (forcible seizure of power) and 327 (public calls for seizure of power), of the Criminal Code; (c) The blanket ban imposed on peaceful demonstrations in key sites in Bishkek since 2022, and the expansion of the ban to other cities, including the city of Osh; (d) Reports that human rights defenders, members of civil society organizations, activists, lawyers and journalists have increasingly become targets of intimidation, surveillance, harassment, threats and reprisals, arbitrary arrest and detention, and violations of their fair trial safeguards, as a consequence of their work.

records.section: Complaints of racial discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes
records.text: 16. The Committee draws the State Party’s attention to its general recommendation No. 31 (2005) on the prevention of racial discrimination in the administration and functioning of the criminal justice system, and recalls that an absence of complaints and legal actions relating to racial discrimination may reveal a lack of suitable legislation, poor awareness of the legal remedies available, a lack of trust in the judicial system, a fear of reprisals or a lack of will on the part of the authorities to prosecute the perpetrators of such acts. It recommends that the State Party: (a) Assess the effectiveness and availability of remedies for victims of racial discrimination and hate crimes and take measures to ensure the availability and accessibility of safe reporting channels and legal aid for these victims; (b) Conduct training programmes for police officers, prosecutors and law enforcement officials on the identification and registration of incidents of racial discrimination and hate crimes, and on the situation of groups exposed to racial discrimination, such as members of ethnic minority groups and non-citizens; (c) Undertake public education campaigns on the rights enshrined in the Convention, on the legal remedies available and on how to file complaints of racial discrimination and hate crimes; (d) Collect statistics, disaggregated by age, gender, and ethnic and national origin, on complaints of racial discrimination and hate crimes, on investigations and prosecutions undertaken, on convictions handed down and sanctions imposed, and on reparations provided to the victims, and include those statistics in its next periodic report.

records.section: Complaints of racial discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes
records.text: 15. The Committee notes the information provided on the investigation and prosecution of 189 cases between 2019 and 2022 on incitement to racial, ethnic, national, religious or interregional hostility pursuant to article 330 of the Criminal Code. Nevertheless, the Committee is concerned about: (a) The lack of information on complaints of racial discrimination pursuant to article 189 of the Criminal Code, including regarding investigations, prosecutions, convictions, and sanctions by domestic courts; (b) The low number of complaints or cases involving hate crimes and hate speech pursuant to article 330 of the Criminal Code, and the lack of disaggregated and detailed information on cases of incitement to racial, ethnic, national, religious or interregional hostility, on prosecutions, and on the convictions and sanctions imposed on the perpetrators of such acts; (c) The lack of information on the recognition and application by the prosecution and domestic courts of racist motivations as aggravating circumstances pursuant to article 74 of the Criminal Code; (d) The lack of information on measures adopted to facilitate access by members of ethnic minority groups and non-citizens to remedies and safe reporting channels, including by means of public education campaigns, and on the provision of legal aid, as recommended by the Committee in its previous concluding observations (arts. 4 and 6).

records.text: 94. Since ratifying the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in 2019, Kyrgyzstan has taken steps to improve the situation of persons with disabilities through law and policy reforms. The pace of reforms was initially slowed down owing to the coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic but is now gathering momentum , with unique opportunities for tangible changes in the lives of persons with disabilities. 95. State authorities have shown interest and commitment to continue on this path, with a particular focus on social protection and increasing the amounts of disability benefits and payments for personal assistants. Such benefits need to be part of a wider system of services and support so that persons with disabilities can be fully integrated into society rather than being relegated as passive recipients of social benefits for their whole lives. The strong economic growth enjoyed by Kyrgyzstan in recent years has created the potential for more ambitious and transformative changes, in particular through the overhaul and design of community-based services and support and making mainstream services and infrastructure accessible. 96. Law and policy changes must be underpinned by a human rights-based approach to disability, with priority given to the reform of the disability assessment system and rejection of the medical model of disability that remains entrenched in legislation, policy, practice and minds. Only by increasing the understanding of the rights of all persons with disabilities and addressing the negative attitudes that persons with disabilities still encounter will law and policy reforms translate into structural and sustainable transformation. All legislation and practices that openly contradict the Convention must be abolished, including the denial of legal capacity, institutionalization and deprivation of liberty on the basis of impairment and on segregation and exclusion from mainstream services , especially in education. 97. Persons with disabilities and their representative organizations are the best allies and experts to assist the Government to advance the process of reform in an accountable, innovative and cost-effective way. Their capacities to monitor and advocate for disability rights should be strengthened, particularly the perspectives of those at greatest risk of exclusion and discrimination , such as persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities, women and girls, older persons and people from rural and remote areas.

records.text: 90. The Special Rapporteur welcomes that inclusiveness was among the key objectives of electoral reforms introduced in Kyrgyzstan over a decade ago. The Central Election Commission actively consults with persons with disabilities and has established a working group on persons with disabilities with the participation of their representative organizations. 91. The Law on Elections guarantees that informational materials about elections and campaign materials are available in various accessible formats. The Central Election Commission reported significant improvements in the accessibility of polling stations equipped with ramps, magnifying glasses and information in Braille. Local authorities and election commissions are also required to map the needs of voters with disabilities and to inspect polling stations before elections to ensure accessibility. 92. Persons with disabilities often face multiple barriers in running and being elected for public office. On the positive side, the Law on Elections requires that political parties include at least two candidates with disabilities on their election lists. The quotas are generally respected at the time of registration of election lists. However, it is reported that candidates with disabilities have been regularly asked by political parties to withdraw and to leave space for other candidates. Therefore, the quota system has had a limited practical impact and persons with disabilities remain largely invisible in the political space. For example, there is only one member of Parliament with disabilities; the member succeeded as an individual candidate in elections following his previous visible participation in Parliament. 93. The Special Rapporteur is concerned that, according to article 3 of the Law on Elections, persons deprived of their legal capacity cannot participate in elections. Persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities, who are thus deprived of their voting rights, in contravention to article 29 of the Convention, are particularly affected in this regard.

records.text: 80. Women and girls with disabilities in Kyrgyzstan, as in most other countries, face multiple barriers to the enjoyment of their human rights compared to men and boys with disabilities and compared to other women and girls. Government officials repeatedly told the Special Rapporteur that they women and girls with disabilities receive equal treatment. However, such gender blindness disregards disproportionate inequalities and discrimination, perpetuating instead of addressing the problem. For this reason, taking measures to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by women and girls with disabilities is a requirement under article 6 of the Convention. 81. The specific challenges faced by and the concerns of women and girls with disabilities are gaining more visibility in Kyrgyzstan, especially through a recent report documenting sexual and gender-based violence against women and girls with disabilities. The situation of women and girls with disabilities was also reflected in the national review of implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action conducted in 2023. 82. Women and girls with disabilities in Kyrgyzstan are at a disproportionately high risk of sexual and gender-based violence. According to the 2024 national review of the implementation of the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, only 14 per cent of women and girls with disabilities feel safe in public places and only 50 per cent feel safe at home. Despite cases of horrific violence and abuse reported by civil society and in the media, few cases appear to have been investigated and prosecuted, and even fewer have led to convictions of the perpetrators and to remedy and reparations for the victims. While some progress has been made in terms of legislation, for example the introduction of harsher sentences for perpetrators of sexual violence against persons with disabilities, more is needed in order to guarantee equal access to justice for survivors, including their protection and social support. 83. The Special Rapporteur repeatedly heard that survivors of violence among persons with disabilities are reluctant to report violence to law enforcement and prosecutorial services as investigative practices provide insufficient protection to victims and deny equal access to justice, including adequate procedural accommodations in place. For instance, survivors are required to confront alleged perpetrators in person during investigations and interrogations are most often led by male officers, who lack awareness of the situation of persons with disabilities and adequate procedures to prevent secondary victimization. Survivors, especially women with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities, face harmful stereotypical attitudes and their statements are likely to be met with disbelief. Furthermore, survivors are subjected to invasive forensic medical examinations and psychiatric evaluations that are incompatible with human rights standards. 84. The significant vulnerabilities faced by many women and girls with disabilities need to be assessed and considered when conducting investigative and judicial proceedings as well as in the design and implementation of protection and support mechanisms for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence. Women and girls with disabilities, particularly in rural and remote areas, face extreme barriers in obtaining protections and support, given their lack of education, dependence on their families and minimal social skills. Inclusive, accessible, and specialized support and protection mechanisms are sparse and are generally made available through non-profit associations without governmental support. 85. During meetings with the Special Rapporteur, women and girls with disabilities also expressed concerns regarding access to medical services, particularly sexual and reproductive health. Reportedly, many women and girls with disabilities have not been examined by a gynaecologist for years owing to lack of awareness, inaccessible facilities and equipment (such as gynaecological chairs and mammogram scanning machines) and discriminatory attitudes on the part of health practitioners. 86. All persons with disabilities, including women and girls, have the right to retain their fertility and to autonomously decide whether and when they want to have children. Enjoying these rights has been a challenge for women and girls with disabilities worldwide, and the Special Rapporteur also heard those concerns during her visit to Kyrgyzstan. 87. Women with disabilities shared personal experiences of being advised to terminate pregnancies by families and medical practitioners. One woman stated that she avoided check‐ups during her pregnancy to avoid pressure from doctors. Reports of involuntary sterilizations were particularly alarming. In one case, a woman was allegedly sterilized after giving birth and found out only when she was not able to become pregnant a second time. The Special Rapporteur was assured that forced sterilization was prohibited under national legislation. However, as women and girls with disabilities often find themselves in vulnerable social and economic situation, they are likely to be more compliant with pressure exerted by families and doctors and less likely to file complaints. In practice, the application of legal rules requires awareness-raising to change societal perceptions and stereotypes. 88. The situation of women and girls with disabilities who have been denied legal capacity is most concerning as their guardians can consent to abortions and contraception on their behalf. In institutions, such as the one for persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities for women and men in Tokmok, female residents are given contraceptive medication based on consultations with relatives. In line with general comment No. 3 (2016) of the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, medical procedures and the administration of contraceptives should only be performed with the free and informed consent of those directly concerned and not based on third-party decisions. In this regard, regulations for supported decision-making and safeguards for free and informed consent need to be put in place. 89. At the time of the visit, the Government was preparing a new regulation on surgical sterilization to outline procedures for conducting voluntary sterilization. However, the text of the draft decree lacked details and safeguards to ensure that informed consent is obtained freely without coercion and information on how related procedures would be adapted and made accessible for persons with different disabilities. Moreover, the draft appeared to allow third-party authorization for sterilization, which is incompatible with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, and included a list of “medical indications”, which particularly concern persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities.

records.text: 72. The right to health is guaranteed in the Constitution of Kyrgyzstan and persons with a certified disability status benefit from free medical services or discounts, depending on the category of their disability status. The Government is focusing on digitalization of services, including introducing tele-medicine, and is planning to build new hospitals in all regions. The new construction plans present a great potential to make healthcare more accessible to persons with disabilities – a key concern expressed by persons with disabilities during the visit of the Special Rapporteur. 73. The Special Rapporteur heard about difficulties in terms of physical accessibility, lack of adapted equipment, attitudinal barriers and discriminatory practices. Specialized medical services are not widely available and persons with disabilities from remote and rural areas face challenges in travelling to the capital, where most specialized services are available. Health professionals reportedly continue to perceive disability from a medical perspective, resulting in dismissive attitudes and inappropriate communication. 74. Persons with hearing impairments voiced concerns regarding access to healthcare, highlighting the fact that emergency medical assistance can only be reached through voice calls. The Special Rapporteur was pleased that the Ministry of Health stated that it was aware of the issue and was working on alternative means of communication with emergency medical services. At present, sign language interpreters are not available in medical facilities, making it difficult for persons with hearing impairments to communicate with health workers directly. One individual indicated that, during a consultation, a medical specialist had refused to communicate with her in writing and insisted that she arrange her own support for interpretation. 75. The Special Rapporteur is concerned that the Law on Health permits the involuntary commitment and treatment in psychiatric hospitals. She recalls that involuntary hospitalization and treatment based on an alleged mental illness or mental disorder contradicts the right liberty and security of person, the principle of free and informed consent, personal integrity and, in some cases, freedom from torture and ill-treatment. National legislation in Kyrgyzstan also allows for wide-ranging limitations of rights in psychiatric hospitals, including the use of the telephone, receiving visitors and the right to have personal items. 76. Rehabilitation services in the country do not meet the needs of persons with disabilities and require significant development in terms of proper facilities, adequate equipment and a specialized labour force. This is a long-term effort; the Special Rapporteur recognizes steps by the Government to improve the availability and accessibility of rehabilitation services by opening a modern multidisciplinary rehabilitation centre for children with disabilities in Bishkek in December 2022. She visited the centre and was pleased to observe that parents are closely involved in rehabilitation sessions so that the children can gain some skills that can be applied at home. In addition, children are offered psychosocial support, respite opportunities and support with legal literacy. 77. Public rehabilitation facilities, especially in remote regions, are often located in older buildings that require renovation and also lack adequate specialists in different therapeutical areas. Information shared with the Special Rapporteur mostly concerned rehabilitation for children with disabilities, leaving open questions about the availability of rehabilitation services for adults. She also heard that public rehabilitation centres mostly cater to persons with physical disabilities, while persons with intellectual disabilities must often rely on costly commercial providers or on non-profit associations. 78. The provision of affordable, quality, user-centred and age-appropriate assistive devices, which is fundamental for personal mobility and independent living, is a requirement under the Convention. This also includes adequately trained personnel to prescribe, fit, train and maintain devices. The right to assistive technology is recognized in article 13 of the Law on the Rights and Guarantees of Persons with Limited Health Functions. However, the list of assistive devices established by the Government does not appear to be easily available. The system to request assistive devices is complicated and is not well-known to users; such devices are not widely available and of good quality. Therefore, many persons with disabilities end up paying out of pocket for assistive technologies or must go without or live with ill-fitting devices, with serious consequences on their day-to-day lives and their health. Electrical wheelchairs, for example, seem almost inexistent. 79. As in other instances, the situation of persons with hearing impairments was particularly striking as all costs related to hearing aids is borne by individuals without governmental assistance. Parents shared stories of having to save money, fundraise and travel abroad for fitting, testing and acquiring hearing aids for their children. She was told that more vendors now offer hearing aids and related services in Kyrgyzstan thanks to efforts of parents of children with hearing impairments. Similarly, cochlear implants are only available through private funding or charities. As such, in the long term, costs associated with parts replacement represent another obstacle for children who received implants.

records.text: 62. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the adoption of the new Law on Education in August 2023. The law represents the most progressive national legislation concerning the rights of persons with disabilities, with references to non-discrimination (including specific reference on the grounds of disability), individualized approaches, support and reasonable accommodation. Most significantly, the right to an inclusive education is guaranteed and applied at all levels of education, with the requirement of an inclusive learning environment, including the training of specialized teaching staff. 63. The new legislation has a transformative potential for the inclusion of persons with disabilities in mainstream education, eventually leading to inclusive employment, economic independence and a disability-inclusive transformation for the whole society. It could mean that the school environment is adapted to the needs of the individual child rather than the child either adapting to the school environment or being excluded from mainstream education. During the visit of the Special Rapporteur, many persons with disabilities and parents of children with disabilities reported that the latter had been their experience. They noted that only children with minor impairments and/or with strong support from their families are able to attend mainstream schools. However, upon reaching secondary education, some children and their families decide to homeschool owing to stigma and lack of an accessible environment in schools. 64. Children with milder cognitive and developmental impairments can access a simplified curriculum in mainstream education. However, according to views shared with the Special Rapporteur, the adapted curricula and textbooks remain too challenging for most children with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities and the general school environment does not have adequate and qualified support systems in place. 65. The Ministry of Education operates 14 boarding schools for 2,281 children with sensory impairments and intellectual and psychosocial disabilities in Kyrgyzstan. The Special Rapporteur visited two such schools (for children with visual and hearing impairments respectively) and was most affected by the curiosity and desire for learning and stimulation expressed by the children she met. 66. She was particularly struck by the situation of children with hearing impairments, who appeared to be taught based on outdated curricula, with grossly inadequate materials, including very old books, pressed to speak orally and were provided with very limited opportunities for extracurricular activities. Alarmingly, special schools for children with hearing impairments do not provide a full curriculum leading up to examinations required to enter university. As a result, they are only given the choice of vocational training for hairdressing, sewing or welding. 67. Children with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities in residential social care institutions have extremely limited access to education and do not follow any specific curricula. Local teachers reportedly visit residential social care institutions to provide limited schooling to those deemed “able to learn”. 68. The Special Rapporteur notes that State officials often referred to homeschooling as a form of inclusive education for children with disabilities. However, homeschooling excludes children form their peers and from the wider community and should only be considered as an exceptional and temporary measure. Moreover, persons with disabilities and parents of children with disabilities repeatedly shared concerns over the quality and monitoring of homeschooling. 69. In higher education, persons with disabilities face significant barriers in terms of accessible environments and adequate support, including for transportation and housing. For the majority, attending university remains prohibitively expensive and complicated. Preferential quotas for State-subsidies university education exist for persons with disabilities but are reportedly not available in the most popular fields of study, such as medicine, law and economics. 70. In this context, the new legal framework on inclusive education should be operationalized as a priority, with adequate strategies, plans, guidelines and funding, and the system of specialized schools for children with disabilities should be discontinued. Confusingly, the Law on Education still includes a category of “special education” for children with disabilities, which leaves the current segregated system in place. The role of the psycho-medical pedagogical commission needs to be reviewed to move from assessing which form of education a child with disabilities should receive towards a multidisciplinary assessment of individual needs and support required for their inclusion in mainstream education. 71. The Special Rapporteur recognizes efforts to introduce digital technologies in education. At the time of her visit, the Ministry of Education was preparing an e-book portal, including adapted e-learning materials, an online testing platform and the equipping of every teacher with a laptop. These efforts could support the implementation of inclusive education, with specific attention to ensure the inclusion of children with disabilities. Such children are more likely to come from poor socioeconomic backgrounds and to lack the resources and skills to use digital technologies.

records.text: 59. Persons with disabilities highlighted barriers to employment as an acute concern during meetings with the Special Rapporteur. The employment rate of persons with disabilities is reportedly alarmingly low, although no official data were available. The Special Rapporteur heard about serious labour discrimination, for example that candidates with disabilities are turned away during interviews once their impairment becomes apparent. 60. The Labor Code of Kyrgyzstan, in chapter 25, provides protections for the right to employment of persons with disabilities, including adjustments and shorter working hours. Such protections should be counterbalanced by concrete incentives for employers to hire persons with disabilities to encourage employers to consider the added value of recruiting persons with disabilities. As far as the Special Rapporteur is aware, there are no reasonable accommodation mechanisms in place to facilitate access for persons with disabilities to the work environment. 61. In a positive development, quotas for the employment of persons with disabilities within civil service are in place and employers are obliged to hire candidates with disabilities referred to them by State employment services. Analysing and assessing the practical impact of the quotas would help to identify shortcomings and promote consideration of how to extend the practice into the private sphere. One concern repeatedly highlighted was that the quotas were filled mainly by persons with minor impairments and did not lead to the inclusion of persons with higher support needs.

records.text: 56. Persons with a certified degree of disability benefit from a pension insurance for disability-related loss of income or from a non-contributory disability cash benefits if they did not participate in pension insurance. Recently, the Government significantly increased the amounts of disability benefits, which, in 2023, ranged between 8,000 to 2,000 som ($92 to $23) depending on the assessed “severity” of disability. This means that many of the benefits still fall well below the minimum subsistence level of 7,900 som. While the disability pensions and social benefits aim to supplement the absence or loss of income, they do not cover the extra costs of living with a disability. 57. The child allowance represents the only poverty alleviation scheme and supports low-income households with children below age 16. The scheme does not consider additional healthcare and other expenses required for children with disabilities among the qualifying parameters. The Special Rapporteur underlines the importance of considering additional disability-related costs in order to effectively address the link between disability and poverty, in particular as the programme is currently under review by the Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs and Migration. 58. Since 2022, low-income families can also receive support through the national social contract programme, with a one-time payment of 100,000 som ($1,150) to start a business and improve their living standards. While the Special Rapporteur was pleased to hear that persons with disabilities were among the beneficiaries of the programme, it appears that there is no priority or quota set for them in the related regulations and they can only apply as a family with children under age 16. Moreover, participation in the programme disqualifies the beneficiaries from continuing to receive social benefits.

records.text: 50. Living independently in the community is a key challenge for persons with disabilities in Kyrgyzstan. There are 17 social residential institutions operated by the Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs and Migration, 11 for adults (total of 1,375 residents) and six for children (348 residents) with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities. Residents cannot freely leave the institutions and follow fixed daily routines. The Special Rapporteur visited three such institutions for persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities, one for adult men, one for adult men and women and one for children. It appeared that the care and other services provided at the institutions was focused on fulfilling basic needs in terms of food, shelter, hygiene and health, but with little to no opportunities for stimulation and learning, especially in the institutions for adults, where residents can spend most of their lives. The institution for children with disabilities in Belovodskoe has been extensively renovated through international donor funding, with visible efforts to provide more rehabilitation opportunities. However, some facilities were clearly not used regularly, mainly due to lack of qualified specialists. 51. Following her visit in 2024, the Special Rapporteur was alarmed to receive reports of extremely poor conditions in some institutions, which could amount to cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment. This calls for urgent investigations and a wider reflection on the overall system in place, including institutionalization in special boarding schools and psychiatric facilities. 52. The Special Rapporteur reiterates that institutionalization, which usually involves denial of legal capacity and constitutes detention and deprivation of liberty based on impairment, is a discriminatory practice against persons with disabilities and therefore infringes on the rights under the Convention. She is concerned that there is no strategy on deinstitutionalization in Kyrgyzstan and discussions on the matter seem to be minimal. Moreover, as recently as 2023, public spending on institutions was increasing and was much larger than the budget for, inter alia, assistive devices. 53. Resources should be channelled into designing and providing community-based services to support independent living, including the provision of an adequate labour force and the use of new technologies. Good alternatives show that, with more individualized approaches, learning of daily skills and peer-to-peer and psychological support, great advances can be made in fostering independent living. The Special Rapporteur was particularly impressed by the support provided to women and girls with disabilities who experienced violence and abuse by an association that provides, inter alia, courses on independent living skills. 54. The programme on personal assistants, introduced in 2018 and extended in 2022, is a step in the right direction, given the transformative potential of personal support for the inclusion of persons with disabilities in all aspects of life. The number of personal assistants significantly increased in recent years, providing support to over 13,000 persons with disabilities in 2024. The programme provides for monthly payments of around $72 to parents or close relatives of persons with disabilities who require constant outside care and supervision, while personal assistants should make every effort to integrate them into society and to adapt socially. Persons with disabilities, and their parents, generally welcomed this programme, particularly as a way of preventing institutionalization. 55. The Special Rapporteur recognizes the good intentions behind the programme and suggests that its framing and objectives should be reviewed to align with the requirements of independent living under the Convention. The current approach risks perpetuating the medicalization and dependency of persons with disabilities. It also places most care and support responsibilities on close relatives, mainly mothers, without providing other sources of support and respite. The programme also significantly limits other employment opportunities for personal assistants as their work schedule should not interfere with providing services to persons with disabilities who require such constant outside care and supervision.

records.section: Legal capacity and access to justice
records.text: 43. The denial of legal capacity, which remains one of the most widespread violations of the human rights of persons with disabilities globally, has extremely serious consequences for the enjoyment of all their other human rights. For that reason, equal recognition before the law is a central element of the Convention. 44. The Special Rapporteur is concerned that Kyrgyzstan has not yet engaged in any substantial reform to abolish legal guardianship for persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities and to introduce a system of supported decision-making. Awareness of this issue seems limited and legal guardianship remains standard practice. 45. The Civil Code contains provisions on legal guardianship for persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities, a measure that severely restricts their freedom to make free choices, including about critical issues such as bodily autonomy, medical treatment and financial transactions. The fact that persons deprived of their legal capacity cannot personally ask for a review of decisions on guardianship (article 296 (2) of the Civil Procedure Code) is most concerning and is a violation of their right to equal recognition before the law, as well as their right to equal and effective access to justice. 46. Deprivation of legal capacity places persons with disabilities at heightened risk of violence, abuse and neglect and only limited information was shared with the Special Rapporteur about procedures and safeguards to prevent and address such risks. While social services are tasked with the monitoring of the living conditions of persons placed under guardianship, the Special Rapporteur was informed that there was an insufficient number of qualified social workers, especially in rural and remote areas, trained on the rights of persons with disabilities. Moreover, the fact that directors of residential institutions for persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities automatically assume legal guardianship for residents raises questions about how their interests and wishes are respected and protected. 47. Persons with disabilities face significant barriers in gaining access to justice owing to a lack of suitable physical, communicational and informational infrastructure allowing them access to police, prosecutors’ and court buildings and services. The Special Rapporteur understands that plans to make courts accessible are under way following a civil court case in 2023 concerning physical inaccessibility of the Osh regional court. 48. Guidelines on procedural and reasonable accommodations during investigations and judicial proceedings, including adequate capacity and resources to effectively provide them, would help to ensure that persons with disabilities have the right to access judicial processes. For instance, it was reported that persons with hearing impairments often have to hire their own sign language interpreters as courts do not have the resources and capacity to do so, despite existing legal obligations. The Special Rapporteur wishes to draw particular attention to the International Principles and Guidelines on Access to Justice for Persons with Disabilities, which provide a human-rights based context and direction in this regard. 49. In the majority of cases, progress in gaining access to justice for persons with disabilities has been achieved through the adoption of the Law on State-guaranteed Legal Aid in 2022, which expanded the right of vulnerable groups, including persons with disabilities, to free legal representation in criminal, administrative and some civil cases. The Government is implementing the law with support from international partners, including by opening free legal aid centres and establishing a hotline for legal assistance. Free legal representation is guaranteed for criminal proceedings, while legal consultations are available in civil cases, including cases of discrimination on the ground of disability.

records.text: 35. Accessibility to the physical, informational and communicational environments and services, including digital technologies, is the backbone to the enjoyment of all rights under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The Special Rapporteur welcomed the fact that the main national policy on the rights of persons with disabilities (the “Accessible Country” programme) is focused on assuring an accessible environment. She was also pleased that senior governmental officials demonstrated understanding that accessibility goes beyond physical infrastructures and includes the informational environment and services so that persons with disabilities can fully participate in society. 36. According to observations shared with the Special Rapporteur, some progress has been achieved in terms of improving the accessible environment Kyrgyzstan in the five years since the ratification of the Convention, notably through building of ramps and the addition of accessible buses in Bishkek. That said, persons with disabilities consistently highlighted challenges in accessing buildings, facilities, transport, services and information as one of the main barriers to the enjoyment and exercise of their rights. The Special Rapporteur herself experienced physical barriers in public spaces, including in gaining access to and inside buildings, shops, restaurants and transportation. 37. While removing such barriers takes time, it is not necessarily as costly and complicated as many assume. In this regard, it should be noted that persons with disabilities can help in providing simple and cost-effective solutions. Initiatives such as the joint accessibility assessment in Bishkek, conducted jointly by public authorities and persons with disabilities in September 2024, are worth replicating to encourage closer collaboration and the sharing of expertise. 38. Legal standards on accessibility, particularly physical accessibility, are in place in Kyrgyzstan, notably through the Law on the Rights and Guarantees of Persons with Limited Health Functions, the Law on Urban Development and Architecture and building codes and regulations. In 2018, the Government adopted two regulations defining the standards and rules for the design and construction of buildings in terms of accessibility for persons with disabilities. These frameworks do not, however, include the key concepts of reasonable accommodation and universal design and only apply to new constructions. 39. Implementation and enforcement of architectural design and construction norms remains a challenge, partially because of lack of expertise and explanatory work with architecture and construction companies. Persons with disabilities cited examples of buildings and facilities, even new ones, that do not meet required standards. Statistics on the number of fines, construction permits stopped or withdrawn and demolitions for non‐compliance with accessibility requirements were not readily available. Overall, monitoring and enforcement of compliance needs to be further strengthened. 40. Furthermore, the commitment to accessibility should be made clear in all public procurement processes for construction and renovation, equipment, supplies and services. This is crucial as the Government is currently investing in major renovations and in building public infrastructure. For example, while the Ministry of Transport and Communications currently includes accessibility as an advantage in the process for the purchase of inter-city buses, it is not listed as a requirement. 41. More capacity and resources are needed to ensure access to information and communication for all persons with disabilities, including sign language interpretation, Braille, easy-to-read formats and augmentative and alternative communication. Although legal guarantees exist for the provision of Braille and sign language interpreters, they are not well implemented owing to lack of resources and qualified personnel. As a result, people with hearing impairment reported that they often have pay out of their own pockets to communicate and access public services; for most people this option is too expensive. 42. The Special Rapporteur welcomes the commitment of the Government to e‐governance, which can greatly improve accessibility to public services for persons with disabilities. She welcomed the adoption of national digital accessibility standards as a significant step forward and supported the prioritization of their implementation.

records.text: 32. According to official statistics in Kyrgyzstan, about 3 per cent of the population, that is, around 217,000 people, have a disability. The data are based on the number of persons with officially recognized disability status – based solely on a medical assessment – and who qualify for cash disability benefits. That number is far below the worldwide estimate that 15 per cent of the population lives with a disability, which means that many persons with disabilities, and their needs, remain invisible in Kyrgyzstan, and that decision-making on policies and public spending on disabilities is not fully driven by facts and data. 33. The Special Rapporteur notes that the purpose of data and statistics goes beyond measuring disability prevalence, constituting a tool to assess the level of inclusion and related barriers to participation in society. That is also the purpose behind the commitment to strengthen data collection and analysis disaggregated by different characteristics, including disability, as part of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. 34. In that context, the Special Rapporteur welcomed the introduction of the Washington Group short set of questions on functioning as part of the most recent population census in Kyrgyzstan in 2022 as a key step towards a fact-based understanding of the situation and needs of persons with disabilities in Kyrgyzstan. At the time of her visit, the census data collected based on the functional limitations was not yet fully processed and analyzed and it was not clear when it would be made publicly available. The Special Rapporteur notes that the preparation phase and common guidance and training of census enumerators is usually key to the successful gathering of data on disability and she suggests focusing further capacity-building and resources in this area in future surveys.

records.text: 25. Some progress has been made towards the participation of persons with disabilities in the formulation and implementation of public policies on disability-related issues, a key principle of the Convention. The Special Rapporteur particularly notes the functioning of the Council for Persons with Disabilities at the governmental level. She was pleased to learn that similar consultative mechanisms exist at the local level, for example in the city of Osh. 26. Participation of persons with disabilities in decision-making, which is a requirement under the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (art. 4 (3)), cannot be effective and meaningful without empowering and supporting organizations of persons with disabilities and activists to advocate for their human rights. The Special Rapporteur particularly recalls the guidance of the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in its general comment No. 7 (2018), outlining the need to strengthen the capacity of organizations of persons with disabilities to participate in all phases of policymaking. The promotion of advocacy by and empowerment of persons with disabilities are key components of their participation in public affairs. 27. In this respect, the Special Rapporteur is seriously concerned about the chilling effect of the adoption of the Law on Foreign Representatives, in April 2024, on all non-profit associations in Kyrgyzstan, including organizations of persons with disabilities. Following its adoption, organizations receiving foreign funding or other resources have been designed as “foreign representatives” and subjected to excessive oversight by public authorities, burdensome reporting obligations and, in the event of non-compliance, face suspension of activities and closure, in violation of the rights to freedoms of association, opinion and expression, privacy and non-discrimination. It is not likely that small and medium-sized organizations, especially at the grassroots level, have the resources and capacity to comply with such onerous bureaucratic requirements. 28. Many organizations and activists voiced alarm over the extremely negative effects of the Law on Advocacy for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, especially as many organizations of persons with disabilities rely on foreign funding for their activities – both to raise awareness and to promote the rights of persons with disabilities, as well as to provide services and support. The imposition of such a high level of control on civil society, including organizations of persons with disabilities, would appear to be rather absurd, in particular given that public authorities themselves actively seek and use foreign funding for capacity‐building, technical assistance, awareness raising, construction and renovation projects and equipment. The Special Rapporteur wishes to recall that, pursuant to article 32 of the Convention, organizations of persons with disabilities should be free to seek and secure funds and resources from national and international donors and States should effectively promote and facilitate their access to foreign funding as part of international cooperation and development aid. 29. Moreover, according to the Law on Foreign Representatives, public authorities have a broad discretion in identifying activities of non-profit associations as “political”, thus undermining their credibility and creating distrust about the activities of organizations that might be advocating for human rights while criticizing governmental policies and measures. Virtually any advocacy and outreach activity can now be interpreted as a political activity, such as organizing public rallies and debates, seeking to influence legislative reforms or disseminating decisions and policies adopted by State bodies, all of which are protected under the right to participate in public affairs, freedom of assembly and freedom of opinion and expression and access to information, including under articles 21 and 29 of the Convention. 30. Instead, the law effectively pushes organizations of persons with disabilities to become charities and service providers and to abstain from the very broad range of activities that can be interpreted as “political” but which are at the core of efforts to advocate for and monitor the rights of persons with disabilities and to participate in public affairs. Tellingly, the law does not identify the social support of persons with disabilities as a political activity, thus reinforcing the outdated and erroneous view of disability as a social issue. 31. Overall, the law is not compatible with the requirement in the Convention to create an enabling environment for the establishment and functioning of organizations of persons with disabilities, including access to both public funding and international cooperation, so that they can effectively participate in public decision-making and monitoring, in accordance with articles 4 (3) and 33 (3) of the Convention. It is critical to include the voices and perspectives of those within the disability community who face multiple forms of discrimination, including women, youth, children, ethnic minorities, persons from rural and remote areas, older persons, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transexual and other gender-diverse persons, refugees and people with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities.

records.section: National implementation, coordination and monitoring mechanisms
records.text: 18. The Ministry of Labour, Social Affairs and Migrationis the focal point for matters relating to the implementation of the Convention. Although other ministries also have competences, including in terms of education, access to justice and healthcare, the Special Rapporteur was not aware of any specific advisers or units in those ministries that would act as sectoral disability specialists. 19. The establishment of the Council for Persons with Disabilities under the Cabinet of Ministers in May 2020 was an important step in elevating the disability agenda within the work of the Government. The Council is a permanent consultative and advisory body composed of members of the Government that meets at least quarterly to develop analysis and recommendations to advance the implementation of State policies related to persons with disabilities. The Special Rapporteur attended a session of the Council, chaired by the Deputy Prime Minister, and was pleased to observe an open interaction between different governmental officials and organizations of persons with disabilities on a range of different topics. In October 2024, the Council established a working group on the rights of children with disabilities. 20. The Council for Persons with Disabilities provides a key platform for consulting persons with disabilities on reforms, policy priorities, progress and concerns. As such, the functioning and work of the Council should be further strengthened and expanded so that it is able to provide policy direction and planning to implement the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Currently, it appears that the agenda of the Council is being developed in an ad hoc manner, based on proposals from its members and without an overarching strategy or coordination. Without a dedicated budget and personnel to assist with providing direction, expertise and follow-up, the role of the Council will remain limited. It should also be clarified as to whether the Council will act as a coordination mechanism under article 33 (1) of the Convention to facilitate intersectoral policy coherence. 21. At present, there is no independent monitoring mechanism mandated to oversee the impact of national policies and strategies on the situation of persons with disabilities or to track progress in the implementation of the Convention. The Special Rapporteur recalls that the State should establish, without delay, an independent monitoring framework, inclusive of persons with disabilities and their representative organizations, in compliance with article 33 (2) of the Convention. 22. The Ombudsman (Akyikatchy) of the Kyrgyz Republic, established by law in 2002, which is responsible, inter alia, for monitoring the protection of human rights in line with the Constitution, laws and international treaties ratified by Kyrgyzstan and the prevention of any form of discrimination, also receives complaints concerning human rights violations. The Special Rapporteur noted the efforts made to protect the human rights of persons with disabilities, mainly by acting on complaints that concern access to social protection allowances, medical assistance, employment and education. The Ombudsman also carries out inspections in public residential institutions accommodating persons with disabilities, including children. 23. However, the legal mandate of the Ombudsman does not specifically focus on the rights of persons with disabilities, which means that there is no consistent monitoring and reporting on all the rights under the Convention, including in its annual reports submitted to Parliament. Additional capacity and resources for the Ombudsman are required in this regard. Moreover, the institution currently has “B” status, indicating that it is not in full compliance with the principles relating to the status of national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights (the Paris Principles). 24. The Special Rapporteur warmly welcomed the work of the National Center for the Prevention of Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (the national preventive mechanism) in monitoring conditions in a range of places of detention and restriction of liberty, including those particularly relevant for persons with disabilities, such as psychiatric hospitals, residential social care institutions and specialized boarding schools. The Special Rapporteur is concerned about reports that the mandate and structure of the Center could be reformed and weakened and she encourages the Government to maintain the independence and adequate resources of this key human rights mechanism.

records.text: 11. The Special Rapporteur recognizes the efforts made by the Government towards legal and policy changes to promote and protect the human rights of persons with disabilities, most notably through the adoption of the “Accessible Country” programme (2023–2030). The programme is aimed at ensuring equal access to the physical environment, infrastructure and services, particularly in the areas of social protection, rehabilitation, labour, education and prosthetic and orthopaedic services. In general, those priorities are in alignment with the key concerns expressed by the persons with disabilities who met with the Special Rapporteur. 12. Importantly, the “Accessible Country” programme recognizes the full scope of accessibility needs for the inclusion of persons with disabilities in society, including the physical, informational and communicational environment, and introduces the concept of universal design and reasonable accommodation. These are foundational building blocks for sustainable progress that merit further elaboration and practical implementation. 13. While the programme represents an important step towards national implementation, it does not cover all the rights and principles of the Convention, nor does it establish legal guarantees. Moreover, nearly 75 per cent of the programme’s budget has not yet been allocated and is expected to be covered through international development cooperation, raising questions about local ownership and sustainable implementation. 14. Implementation of the Convention is a whole-of-society change and therefore touches upon many laws and policies. As such, a more ambitious plan will eventually be required to systematically review and reform existing laws and policies. The Special Rapporteur heard that some laws have been updated, such as the Law on Education. A more comprehensive and coherent approach is needed, starting with amending and/or replacing the 2008 Law on the Rights and Guarantees of Persons with Limited Health Functions, which frames disability from a medical perspective and overlooks the role of social barriers in creating disabilities. For instance, the law contains an article on “prevention and avoidance of disability”, which reinforces the perception of disability as a medical problem. 15. The Special Rapporteur recognized attempts to introduce a new law on the rights of persons with disabilities and welcomed that consultations on a new draft initiated by members of Parliament were to start shortly after her visit. Indeed, the adoption of a new law should be a key priority going forward. The process should ensure an inclusive and participatory drafting process that includes persons with disabilities and their representative organizations, covering all disabilities, as well as groups such as women and children with disabilities, in full compliance with the Convention. 16. National development strategies aimed at implementing the Sustainable Development Goals offer an important policy framework for change; disability inclusion should be mainstreamed throughout the implementation of the Goals, in accordance with the principle of “leaving no one behind”, and as specifically addressed in several targets and indicators. 17. The National Development Strategy of Kyrgyzstan (2018–2040) incorporates the Sustainable Development Goals and adheres to the commitment to “leaving no one behind”. It contains priority measures and tasks to strengthen social protections and support for disadvantaged groups, including persons with disabilities. However, disability inclusion does not appear to be mainstreamed or specifically addressed in other areas, such as education and employment. The 2025 voluntary national review process, to which Kyrgyzstan has committed, provides a good opportunity to strengthen disability inclusion in national development policies and in their review and to ensure that persons with disabilities are consulted throughout the process.

records.section: Foundations for implementing the Convention Anti-discrimination and combating stigma
records.text: 8. Discrimination on the ground of disability is specifically prohibited in the Constitution of Kyrgyzstan (article 24). However, there is no comprehensive equality and anti‐discrimination law in place and protections against multiple and intersecting forms of discrimination are lacking. While the Law on the Rights and Guarantees of Persons with Limited Health Functions (2008) refers to anti-discrimination as a principle of State policy, it neither prohibits such discrimination nor does it impose a duty to take measures to prevent discrimination on the grounds of disability. As such, the anti-discrimination framework remains underdeveloped and without the effective legal protections that would ensure systemic change and the promotion and protection of the human rights of persons with disabilities. 9. In that context, most tangible changes in terms of anti-discrimination appear to be driven through civil lawsuits seeking the recognition of rights and individual remedies, for example on access to physical infrastructure, including transport, and to services. Litigating for equal rights and opportunities requires significant resources and time, which, coupled with barriers to access justice for persons with disabilities, means that only a small number of cases concerning discriminatory practices are contested in court and are properly redressed. 10. While persons with disabilities are becoming more visible in society following the ratification of the Convention, especially persons with physical and sensory impairments, negative attitudes and stigma persist, affecting, in particular, women and girls, persons with intellectual and psychosocial disabilities and people in rural and remote areas. The Special Rapporteur was told about cases of persons with disabilities, especially women and girls, who had no birth records and had been isolated by their families in rural areas and persons with disabilities shared difficulties experienced renting housing or finding employment.

The Committee acknowledges the measures taken to address the negative impact of frequent natural disasters on the availability of food and the measures taken by the State party to improve access to adequate food and nutrition through international technical cooperation. The Committee notes with concern reports indicating that about three out of four households in the State party cannot afford an adequate diet or to consume nutrient-rich foods, with the most of their calorie intake being based on wheat, potatoes and sugar (arts. 11 and 12).

The Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Enact legislation and a comprehensive regulatory framework on human rights due diligence, making it compulsory for State-owned and private business enterprises operating or domiciled in the State party’s jurisdiction to identify, prevent, mitigate and address environmental harm and abuses of economic, social and cultural rights in their operations; (b) Expedite the adoption of the draft national action plan on business and human rights, ensuring broad consultations with civil society, social partners, experts and the local population, taking into account the “ Guidance on national action plans on business and human rights ” of the Working Group on the issue of human rights and transnational corporations and other business enterprises; (c) Carry out systematic and independent human rights and environmental impact assessments, in consultation with affected communities, in the context of large ‐ scale development, investment and natural resource exploitation projects, and provide information to the public, in a transparent and comprehensive manner, on the impact of such projects on the enjoyment of economic, social and cultural rights and on the environment, in particular regarding activities related to the geological study of extractive resources for the purpose of prospecting, exploration and development of uranium and thorium deposits; (d) Be guided by the Committee’s general comment No. 24 (2017) on State obligations under the Covenant in the context of business activities.

records.section: Business and economic, social and cultural rights
records.text: 12. While noting the efforts to develop a national action plan to implement the Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, the Committee is concerned about the absence of a regulatory framework that foresees legal obligations for businesses under the State party’s jurisdiction to exercise human rights due diligence. The Committee expresses concern about the detrimental impact of extractive activities and development projects on the environment and livelihoods of local communities, and notes with concern that there are no effective human rights and environmental impact assessments and consultations with affected local communities. The Committee also expresses concern about the persistent adverse effects of industrial pollution and ground contamination, noting that the law of 2019 on the prohibition of activities related to the geological study of subsurface resources for the purpose of prospecting, exploration and development of uranium and thorium deposits was repealed on 13 June 2024 without public consultations with affected communities.

The Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Revise, in consultation with civil society, its legislative framework, including the existing Non-Profit Organizations Act, so as to remove the disproportionate and discriminatory obligation of being registered in the Registry of Non-Profit Organizations Performing Functions of Foreign Representatives if a civil society organization receives foreign funding and is engaged in broadly worded “ political activities ” , abolish undue restrictions on civil society organizations’ operational autonomy, including the extrajudicial suspension of their operations by the Ministry of Justice and eventual liquidation through a court suit , and ensure that the State party’s laws and policies guarantee an environment in which civil society organizations are enabled to freely carry out their activities without undue control, interference or restrictions; (b) Ensure that the draft law on mass media is adopted by the parliament as revised in close consultation with civil society and media representatives, and ensure that the State party’s legislative framework enables favourable conditions for journalists and media outlets to carry out their activities without undue control, interference or restrictions; (c) Effectively address cases of harassment, intimidation and reprisals against journalists and human rights defenders by government authorities and private persons or entities, and prevent cases of judicial harassment against them, ensuring that the State party’s laws are not used to prosecute and punish them for their legitimate activities; (d) Be guided by the Committee’s statement on human rights defenders and economic, social and cultural rights.

records.text: 10. Noting the prosecution of human rights defenders in relation to their participation in peaceful protests, the Committee remains concerned about: (a) The disproportionate obligations under the Non-Profit Organizations Act, as amended in April 2024, that require all non-profit organizations created on the territory of the State party that receive foreign funding and engage in broadly worded “political activities” to register in the public Registry of Non-Profit Organizations Performing Functions of Foreign Representatives, label all materials as disseminated “by a foreign representative” and submit annual audit reports in addition to other reports required under the law; (b) The disproportionate obligations and undue restrictions on journalists and media outlets that were proposed in the previous version of the draft law on mass media, while noting that a revised version with input from civil society and the media is currently under consideration by the presidential administration; (c) The reports of harassment, intimidation and reprisals against, as well as cases of arrests, detention and trials of, journalists and human rights defenders, including those working to defend economic, social and cultural rights and those advocating for the rights of minorities and LGBTQI+ persons.

The Committee recommends that the State party take all measures necessary to ensure the impartiality and independence of the judiciary, as a means of safeguarding the enjoyment of human rights, including economic, social and cultural rights. In particular, it recommends that the State party address corruption in the judiciary and take legislative measures to prevent undue interference by the executive and legislative bodies in the activities of the judiciary, in particular in the selection, appointment and removal of judges and with respect to non-interference in the decisions of the Constitutional Court. The Committee refers the State party to the Basic Principles on the Independence of the Judiciary and the Guidelines on the Role of Prosecutors, and to the Human Rights Committee’s related recommendation.

The Committee expresses concern that, under the law of 2023 on amendments to the law on the Constitutional Court, the President can request the Constitutional Court to revise and annul its decisions, including in cases where the President finds a decision of the Constitutional Court to be in contravention of the moral values or public consciousness of the people of Kyrgyzstan.

records.section: Illegal or clandestine movements and employment of migrant workers in an irregular situation
records.text: 52. Recalling its previous recommendations, the Committee recommends that the State party, in accordance with the Recommended Principles and Guidelines on Human Rights and Human Trafficking of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights ( OHCHR ) and with target 5.2 of the Sustainable Development Goals: (a) Implement the Cabinet of Ministers Programme to Combat Trafficking in Persons for 2022–2025 and the action plan for its implementation, ensuring its full compatibility with the Convention and the allocation of adequate resources, and ensur e that it addresses the root causes of trafficking in persons ; (b) Enhance the guidelines for the early identification of victims of trafficking and reinforce the mechanisms of support, referral, rehabilitation and social integration for victims, including by providing them with access to shelters and legal, medical and psychosocial assistance; (c) Ensure that child victims of trafficking are provided with appropriate assistance and protection , with full account taken of their special rights and needs; (d) Ensure prompt, effective and impartial investigation, prosecution and punishment in all cases of trafficking in persons and other related offences; (e) Strengthen training, including on gender-responsive and child-friendly approaches, for law enforcement officials, judges, prosecutors, labour inspectors, teachers, health - care workers and the staff of the State party’s embassies and consulates, and more widely disseminate information on trafficking in persons and assistance for victims, while ensuring a multidisciplinary approach; (f) Step up awareness-raising and information campaigns on the prevention of trafficking in migrant workers and encourage the private sector to protect persons from all forms of exploitation, including forced labour and services; (g) Systematically collect disaggregated data on trafficking in persons, including data on all forms of exploitation, with a view to preventing such trafficking; (h) Continue to strengthen international, regional and bilateral cooperation through agreements with countries of origin, transit and destination on preventing and combating trafficking in persons; (i) Provide in its next periodic report data on trafficking, prostitution and other exploitation of women and girls, the number of prosecutions and convictions in cases of trafficking and sexual exploitation, and the impact of the measures taken to combat these phenomena.

records.text: 49. The Committee is concerned about reports that Kyrgyz migrant workers and members of their families face discriminatory attitudes and are often targets of hate crimes and xenophobic assaults in the main countries of employment, in particular in the Russian Federation. The Committee is particularly concerned about the lack of protection of Kyrgyz migrant workers abroad from violations of their rights, including arbitrary detention and expulsion and deprivation of liberty in temporary immigration detention centres, and about the lack of protection from recruitment as mercenaries in the Russian Federation. The Committee is also concerned about the lack of information regarding cultural initiatives for the community of Kyrgyz migrant workers, including online courses on the Kyrgyz language and history.

However, the Committee remains concerned that this general entitlement to free legal aid applies only in criminal proceedings, and is therefore limited in civil and administrative proceedings to Kyrgyz citizens only. The Committee is also concerned that no information has been provided on the number of cases or proceedings brought by migrant workers and members of their families, including those in an irregular situation, which may reflect a lack of awareness on their part of their rights and of legal remedies available to them.

With reference to its previous recommendations, the Committee recommends that the State party: (a) Adopt comprehensive legislation prohibiting all forms of discrimination, in compliance with the Convention and other relevant international instruments; (b) Take all the measures necessary to amend legislation to ensure that migrant workers living with HIV/AIDS are able to obtain a work permit; (c) Ensure that all migrant workers and members of their families, in both regular and irregular situations, within its territory or subject to its jurisdiction enjoy, without discrimination, the rights recognized by the Convention, in accordance with article 7 thereof, both in law and in practice; (d) Take proactive measures to eliminate discriminatory stereotypes about migrant workers and members of their families, in political discourse and in the media, by strictly applying criminal law provisions and raising awareness among law enforcement officials, politicians, journalists and the general public as to the discriminatory nature of such stereotypes ; (e) Provide information in its next periodic report on the measures taken to improve and implement its legislative framework on non-discrimination as regards the rights of migrant workers and members of their families, irrespective of their status.
